title: Whether and How Parental‐Adolescent Attachment and Peer Attachment Relate to the Development of Self‐Control in Adolescents: A Random Intercept Cross‐Lagged Panel Analysis
abstract: ABSTRACT Self‐control denotes the capacity to intentionally pursue actions that align with long‐term, meaningful goals. Although cumulative evidence has shown that parental‐adolescent attachment and peer attachment are closely associated with self‐control, the longitudinal links between mother attachment, father attachment, peer attachment, and self‐control are unclear. This study utilized Random‐Intercept Cross‐Lagged Panel Models (RI‐CLPMs) to analyse longitudinal data from 1312 Chinese adolescents (age range 12–18, M age = 14.29, SD = 1.38; 50.2% boys) over 1 year with three measurements (i.e., 6 months apart across three cohorts). After separating within‐person and between‐person associations, the results from the RI‐CLPMs revealed that, at the between‐person level, both parental‐adolescent attachment (including attachment to both mother and father) and peer attachment were positively associated with self‐control. At the within‐person level, cross‐lagged effects were found between mother attachment and self‐control. Additionally, self‐control was found to positively predict subsequent father attachment and peer attachment. Furthermore, father attachment at T2 positively predicted self‐control at T3, while peer attachment at T1 positively predicted self‐control at T2. The differing findings regarding mother attachment, father attachment, and peer attachment highlight the importance of considering various significant figures in the study of attachment and self‐control.
